title: Apple Releases New AI Health App
content:
Apple today launched a new research study in the U.S. to explore the use of AI for health, and it has released a dedicated iPhone app for participants.
In a press release, Apple said the study and app are "designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools."
The Apple Health AI Study App contains a generative AI chatbot that participants can use to ask questions about their health, with answers accompanied by links to peer-reviewed clinical citations where necessary. Apple said the study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, described as a leading clinical AI platform.
"By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension, and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry," said Apple.
For more details about the study, read our coverage of Apple's announcement.
Here is the App Store description for the Apple Health AI Study App:
Help Apple build better health AI products.
Join the Apple Health Al Usage Study and help us explore how Al can support you in understanding your health. When you join the study, you'll get access to a custom app built on technology from OpenEvidence, an Al platform trained on peer-reviewed medical research and clinical guidelines. Ask the app all your health questions and get answers personalized to you based on Apple Health data you choose to share.
Any time you have a health question, ask the app. You can use it to:
• Understand symptoms or conditions
• Put your personal Health data in context
• Prepare for a medical visit
• Build a personalized exercise or meal plan
Questions you ask support research that can help Apple make health Al smarter for everyone.
Neither the app nor the research study provides medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Consult a medical professional to address health concerns or verify information.
The study is open to up to 200,000 eligible U.S. residents who are 21 or older. Participants must have an iPhone 15 Pro or newer running iOS 26 or later.

report.summary: Apple launched a U.S. research study and iPhone app that uses a conversational health AI built with OpenEvidence to study trust, response quality, and user behavior.
report.background: Apple has steadily expanded its health footprint through the Health app, Apple Watch sensors, and research initiatives. The new study moves Apple into conversational health AI, a area where users increasingly ask chatbots about symptoms, medications, and lifestyle choices, but where accuracy, trust, privacy, and clinical grounding remain unresolved. Apple is partnering with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform trained on peer-reviewed medical research and guidelines, to provide a more evidence-backed chatbot experience. The study is designed to observe how people interact with such tools, what builds trust, whether responses are understood, and how answers influence everyday health actions. The limited, opt-in U.S. study also reflects Apple’s cautious approach: the app is a research tool, not a medical device, and it explicitly does not provide diagnosis or treatment. The results could shape how Apple and the wider industry design responsible health AI experiences.
key_points: Apple released a dedicated iPhone app for a U.S. research study open to up to 200,000 eligible residents aged 21 or older. Participants need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer running iOS 26 or later, reflecting the computing demands of on-device and conversational AI features.

The app contains a generative AI chatbot built on OpenEvidence technology, which is trained on peer-reviewed medical research and clinical guidelines. Answers can include links to clinical citations where necessary, and can be personalized using Apple Health data that participants choose to share.

The study examines what drives user trust, response quality, comprehension, and everyday health actions. Apple says the goal is to inform responsible design of health AI experiences for itself and the industry, rather than to launch a consumer medical product.

Apple stresses that neither the app nor the study provides medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Participants are told to consult medical professionals for health concerns or to verify information, a sign of the regulatory and safety boundaries around health AI.

The launch signals Apple’s interest in moving health features beyond passive tracking toward conversational assistance. By limiting the study to invited eligible participants and citing clinical sources, Apple is testing health AI carefully before any broader consumer release.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Apple’s study validates citation-backed clinical chatbots as a serious research direction. It highlights that trust, comprehension, and real-world behavior matter as much as model accuracy, and it could push health AI developers toward evidence-linked answers, clearer safety language, and privacy-preserving personalization. For developers, the app points to opportunities around HealthKit integration, clinical retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation frameworks, and consent-driven data sharing, but also to strict limits around medical claims. For regular users, the study suggests future health tools may offer more conversational, personalized guidance grounded in medical literature. However, access is limited, the app is not a doctor, and participants must weigh convenience against health-data privacy. The results may shape how cautiously or quickly Apple brings such features to mainstream users.
report.tools: Follow OpenEvidence, the clinical AI platform powering the study’s chatbot, for evidence-linked medical answers. Apple Health and HealthKit are relevant for developers exploring consent-based personalization and health-data workflows. Watch Apple’s ResearchKit and Health Studies app ecosystem for future research-app patterns. For builders, clinical RAG and citation-verification tooling, plus privacy-preserving evaluation frameworks, are worth monitoring as health AI moves from demos to regulated, trust-sensitive products.
